newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: RUGBY UNION-NEW CONTROVERSY ROCKS SOUTH AFRICAN RUGBY.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-NEW CONTROVERSY ROCKS SOUTH AFRICAN RUGBY.

text.p: South African rugby, stunned by a scandal over racism, could face the added embarrassment of a commission of inquiry if it refuses to cooperate with a government probe of alleged financial irregularities.

The South African Rugby Football Union's (SARFU) executive committee was due to meet sports minister Steve Tshwete in Cape Town on Friday, when the scope of the task force investigation would be outlined.
However, the presence of a member of the National Olympic Committee of South Africa (NOCSA) on the task force has angered SARFU. The Union are not members of NOCSA nor is rugby an Olympic sport.
According to a SARFU spokesman on Wednesday, the union was sticking to its objections and preparing to boycott the meeting.

"If they do not attend the meeting we will take the appropriate steps and they will not get the report," ministerial spokeswoman Zipporah Mothoa said, referring to a dossier which raises questions about the financial handling of sponsorship and television deals in the game.
"The minister (Tshwete) invited the SARFU executive committee to meet him so he could explain the task force and all its implications," she said.
"Rian Oberholzer (chief executive) and Hennie Erasmus (executive committee member) agreed that would be fine. As far as we are concerned we are to meet them on Friday," Mothoa told Reuters.
She declined to elaborate on what action might be taken against SARFU if it refused to cooperate, but it could include their worst-case scenario of a commission of inquiry.
Last week, after the task force was announced, Oberholzer expressed relief that a full scale commission had not been appointed.

An official inquiry would deal another body blow to South African rugby, dragged through the mud this week when national Springboks team coach Andre Markgraaff was forced to resign for referring to black members of the National Sports Council as "fucking kaffirs" -- a term of gross abuse in South Africa.

The report due to be discussed on Friday refers to a dossier prepared by former Transvaal Rugby Union vice-president Brian van Rooyen which alleges financial irregularities involving sponsorships and television deals.
Tshwete, ignoring threats of legal action from SARFU president Louis Luyt, has said he will release the report to SARFU "when the time is right".
SARFU press officer Alex Broun reiterated the union's stance on Wednesday: "It doesn't look like a meeting will take at the moment," he told Reuters.

"We have an obligation to our sponsors and television rights holding broadcasters to protect their interests and we do not feel it is appropriate to have representatives from other sporting codes probing into SARFU matters."
The government appointed Pickard Commission recently uncovered "gross mismanagement" in South African football which led directly to the resignation of Football Association president Stix Morewa.
